entries.meaning: Sītā came and bowed at the eminent sage’s feet, receiving the fitting blessing her heart desired. She met the guru’s wife and the wives of the sages; their love cannot be told. Bowing again and again at every woman’s feet, she obtained words of blessing dear to her heart. When all her mothers-in-law beheld Sītā—delicate and frightened, eyes closed—they thought her like a swan fallen into a hunter’s power and lamented the Creator’s crooked deed. Looking upon her, they felt utter pain, yet one must endure whatever fate imposes. Janaka’s daughter then steadied her heart, though her blue-lotus eyes filled with water, and went to meet each mother-in-law; compassion covered the earth at that moment. Sītā touched each one’s feet and embraced her with profound love; overcome by affection, the women inwardly blessed her to live forever full of married felicity.

Seeing Sītā and all the queens distraught with affection, the wise guru asked everyone to sit. The chief sage explained the illusory course of the world and related a little teaching about the highest truth. Then he told of the king’s departure to heaven. Hearing it, Raghunātha suffered unbearable grief; reflecting that his own love had caused the death, even the steadfast bearer of courage became deeply shaken. At the thunderbolt-hard, bitter news, Lakṣmaṇa, Sītā, and all the queens wailed, and the entire company sank in sorrow as though the realm had met disaster that day. The eminent sage again consoled Rāma, and the company bathed in the sacred river. The Lord kept a waterless fast that day, and at the sage’s instruction no one drank. At dawn Raghunandana reverently performed every rite the sage ordered, joined with faith and devotion.

Rāma performed his father’s rites exactly as the Vedas prescribe and became ritually pure, though his own name is the fire that burns the cotton of sin and, when remembered, the source of every blessing. The one who purifies even holy places, as the Gaṅgā invoked into them does, became pure because convention approved it. After two days of observance, Rāma lovingly told his guru: ‘Lord, all these people are utterly distressed, living only on tubers, roots, fruit, and water. For me, a moment spent seeing Bharata, Śatrughna, the ministers, and all the mothers pass like an age. Please return to the city with everyone, while I remain here; you are like Indra in Amarāvatī. In saying so much I have acted boldly—please do whatever is fitting.’ The guru replied: ‘How could Rāma, bridge of duty and abode of compassion, speak otherwise? Let the grieving people find relief by seeing you for two more days.’

Hearing Rāma’s words, the assembly grew afraid, like a distressed ship in the ocean; hearing the guru’s reply, it felt an auspicious wind arise. Three times each day people bathed in the sacred water whose mere sight destroys floods of sin. Filling their eyes with the embodiment of blessing, they joyfully gazed upon Rāma and repeatedly prostrated. They explored Rāma’s mountain and forest, where every joy was present and every sorrow absent. Cascades poured nectar-like water and a threefold breeze dispelled the three afflictions. Trees, vines, and grasses of countless kinds carried fruit, flowers, and many-colored shoots; beautiful rocks and pleasant shade stood everywhere. Who could describe that woodland beauty? Lotuses filled ponds where waterbirds called and bees hummed; many-colored forest animals and birds roamed with enmity gone.

Kols, Kirātas, Bhils, and other forest dwellers brought pure, lovely honey sweet as nectar. Again and again they filled and arranged handsome leaf cups with tubers, roots, fruit, and tender shoots. Bowing humbly, they offered these to everyone, explaining each item’s taste, variety, virtue, and name. The citizens offered high prices, but the forest people accepted nothing and, when gifts were pressed upon them, invoked Rāma and returned them. Immersed in affection they said gently, recognizing holy love: ‘You are virtuous; we low Niṣādas have gained Rāma’s sight only through grace. Seeing you is exceedingly inaccessible to us, like a stream of the celestial river upon desert ground. Compassionate Rāma honored the Niṣāda; a king should care for family and subjects. Knowing this in your hearts, abandon reserve, accept our affection, and take these fruits, grasses, and shoots so that we may become fulfilled.’

The forest people continued: ‘You are beloved guests who have set foot in the forest, but service worthy of you lies beyond our fortune. What can we give you, masters? Firewood and leaves are a Kirāta’s friendship. Our greatest service is merely not to steal your vessels and clothes. We are dull creatures, killers of living beings, crooked, ill-conducted, ill-minded, and low-born. Night and day pass in sin; we have no cloth at the waist and our bellies are never filled. How could anyone among us possess even dreamlike awareness of duty? This change is the effect of seeing Raghunandana. From the moment we beheld the Lord’s lotus feet, our unbearable sorrows and faults disappeared.’ Hearing these words, the townspeople filled with love and began praising the forest dwellers’ fortune.

The city’s women were absorbed in intense love, and whole days passed like moments. Sītā assumed a form suited to each mother-in-law and served each with equal reverence; no one but Rāma perceived the secret, for all illusion rests within Sītā’s own power. Through loving service Sītā brought the mothers under her affection, and they gave her happiness, instruction, and blessings. Seeing Sītā and the two simple-hearted brothers, the crooked queen repented to exhaustion and begged the earth to receive her; but earth gave no opening and destiny no death. Poets say, as known in world and Veda, that one opposed to Rāma finds no place even in hell. A doubt occupied every mind: would destiny send Rāma to Ayodhyā or not? Bharata slept neither at night nor ate by day, but remained absorbed in pure anxiety, like a fish sinking into vile mud as its water dwindles.

Bharata thought: ‘Time has worked a crooked design under cover of my mother, like a crop of rice ripening amid calamity and fear. How can Rāma’s consecration occur? In my confusion I see not one device. He must return in obedience to the guru; the sage will speak again after learning Rāma’s preference. If his mother asks, Raghurāya may return—but will Rāma’s mother insist? I am merely a follower; how much does my word count when hostile destiny has made the moment adverse? If I insist, it would be utter wrongdoing, for a servant’s duty is weightier than Mount Kailāsa.’ No single strategy settled in his mind, and the night passed in thought. At dawn he bathed, bowed his head to the Lord, and sat when summoned by the sages. With permission he saluted the guru’s lotus feet and took his seat as brahmins, citizens, ministers, and assembly members gathered.

The eminent sage spoke suitably to the occasion: ‘Listen, assembly and discerning Bharata. Rāma is the sun of the Solar line, sovereign lord of duty, self-mastered king, and God. True to his word, guardian of revelation’s bridge, he was born for the world’s welfare. He follows the words of guru, father, and mother, destroys the wicked, and benefits the gods. No one understands policy, love, the highest good, and practical interest as truly as Rāma. Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, moon, sun, guardians of directions, illusion, living beings, action, cosmic serpent, earth—every power up to Time, and the yogic perfections praised by scripture, all stand beneath Rāma’s command. Reflect inwardly and see clearly: his will rests upon every head. Our welfare comes by honoring Rāma’s command and inclination. Wise ones, understand this and together approve what accords with it.’

The sage continued: ‘Rāma’s consecration would gladden everyone; it is the single path and root of blessing and joy. Consider how Raghurāya may return to Ayodhyā and tell what means should be adopted.’ Everyone respectfully heard speech imbued with policy, highest good, and practical interest but, bewildered, found no answer. Bharata then bowed his head, joined his hands, and said: ‘Many kings have arisen in the Solar line, each greater than the last. Father and mother give everyone birth, while the Creator assigns actions auspicious and inauspicious. The world knows that your blessing destroys sorrow and prepares every welfare. But when even such a master’s purpose is blocked by destiny’s course, who can overturn the stance destiny has taken? Ask me what means remain—yet all this is my misfortune.’ Hearing his loving words, affection surged in the guru’s heart.
